claim: Aging is associated with central fat redistribution and insulin resistance.
source: Aging is associated with central fat redistribution and insulin resistance.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about aging.

claim: Increased cell passages of young-donor ASCs (in vitro aging) resulted in senescence but not oxidative stress.
source: Increased cell passages of young-donor ASCs (in vitro aging) resulted in senescence but not oxidative stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing senescence markers increased with passage number while ROS levels remained unchanged in young-donor ASCs.

claim: ASC-derived adipocytes from young-donor ASCs at increased passages presented impaired adipogenesis but no early mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: ASC-derived adipocytes presented impaired adipogenesis but no early mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing decreased lipid accumulation and adipogenic markers in differentiated cells from young-donor ASCs at later passages, while mitochondrial function was preserved at P7.

claim: Aged-donor ASCs at early passages displayed oxidative stress and mild senescence.
source: Conversely, aged-donor ASCs at early passages displayed oxidative stress and mild senescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of ROS production and senescence markers in aged-donor ASCs at P3.

claim: ASC-derived adipocytes from aged-donor ASCs exhibited oxidative stress and early mitochondrial dysfunction but adipogenesis was preserved.
source: ASC-derived adipocytes exhibited oxidative stress, and early mitochondrial dysfunction but adipogenesis was preserved.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased ROS, altered mitochondrial function, but similar lipid accumulation in adipocytes differentiated from aged-donor ASCs at P3.

claim: In vitro aging of aged-donor ASCs resulted in further increased senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and severe adipocyte dysfunction.
source: In vitro aging of aged-donor ASCs resulted in further increased senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and severe adipocyte dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing progressive worsening of all measured parameters in aged-donor ASCs cultured to later passages.

claim: Metformin treatment of in vitro aged young-donor ASCs did not alleviate any alterations.
source: When in vitro aged young-donor ASCs were treated with metformin, no alteration was alleviated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing metformin had no significant effect on senescence markers, oxidative stress, or adipogenic capacity in young-donor ASCs.

claim: Metformin treatment of aged-donor ASCs decreased oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction resulting in decreased senescence.
source: Conversely, metformin treatment of aged-donor ASCs decreased oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction resulting in decreased senescence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing metformin reduced ROS production, improved mitochondrial function, and decreased senescence markers in aged-donor ASCs.

claim: Metformin's prevention of oxidative stress and resulting senescence improved the cells' adipogenic capacity and insulin sensitivity.
source: Metformin's prevention of oxidative stress and of the resulting senescence improved the cells' adipogenic capacity and insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing improved lipid accumulation and insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in adipocytes differentiated from metformin-treated aged-donor ASCs.

claim: Metformin's effect was mediated by the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase.
source: This effect was mediated by the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase as revealed by its specific inhibition and activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that compound C (AMPK inhibitor) blocked metformin's effects and AICAR (AMPK activator) mimicked them.

claim: Aging ASC-derived adipocytes presented impaired adipogenesis and insulin sensitivity.
source: Overall, aging ASC-derived adipocytes presented impaired adipogenesis and insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Targeting stress-induced senescence of ASCs with metformin may improve age-related adipose tissue dysfunction.
source: Targeting stress-induced senescence of ASCs with metformin may improve age-related adipose tissue dysfunction.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings with metformin in aged-donor ASCs.

claim: Aging is physiologically associated with fat redistribution and a metabolic and functional decline in adipose tissue, associated with oxidative stress, inflammation, and fibrosis.
source: Aging is physiologically associated with fat redistribution and a metabolic and functional decline in adipose tissue, associated with oxidative stress, inflammation, and fibrosis (Cartwright et al., 2007; Kuk et al., 2009; Cartwright et al., 2010; Tchkonia et al., 2010; Luo and Liu, 2016; Stout et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The age-related redistribution of adipose tissue is characterized by the accumulation of truncal fat, hypertrophy of visceral adipose tissue (VAT), and overall loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue (SCAT).
source: The age-related redistribution of adipose tissue is characterized by the accumulation of truncal fat, hypertrophy of visceral adipose tissue (VAT), and overall loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue (SCAT) (Oikawa et al., 2016; Park et al., 2016; Mancuso and Bouchard, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: An excess amount of VAT might reflect the paucity of SCAT during aging.
source: An excess amount of VAT might reflect the paucity of SCAT during aging.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the relationship between VAT and SCAT during aging.

claim: A decline in SCAT storage capacity might lead to ectopic lipid deposition in the bone marrow, heart, liver, and muscles and an increase in cardiometabolic comorbidities.
source: Indeed, while accumulation of SCAT in the lower part of the body is considered to be a metabolic sink capable of buffering surplus energy, a decline in SCAT storage capacity might lead to (i) ectopic lipid deposition in the bone marrow, heart, liver, and muscles and (ii) an increase in cardiometabolic comorbidities (Stout et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about the consequences of SCAT decline.

claim: Appropriate SCAT plasticity and expandability guard against metabolic disorders (including insulin resistance).
source: Accordingly, it has been suggested that appropriate SCAT plasticity and expandability guard against metabolic disorders (including insulin resistance) and that the age-related loss of these properties favors metabolic disorders (Pasarica et al., 2009; McLaughlin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The age-related loss of SCAT plasticity and expandability favors metabolic disorders.
source: Accordingly, it has been suggested that appropriate SCAT plasticity and expandability guard against metabolic disorders (including insulin resistance) and that the age-related loss of these properties favors metabolic disorders (Pasarica et al., 2009; McLaughlin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Failure of SCAT is likely to result from the impaired recruitment of precursors and blunted adipogenesis.
source: Failure of SCAT is likely to result from the impaired recruitment of precursors and blunted adipogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanisms underlying SCAT failure.

claim: The identification of adipose-derived progenitor cells in the stromal vascular fraction of adipose tissue has highlighted the importance of de novo adipogenesis in adipose tissue expansion.
source: The identification of adipose-derived progenitor cells in the stromal vascular fraction of adipose tissue has highlighted the importance of de novo adipogenesis in adipose tissue expansion (Cawthorn et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: ASCs are defined as plastic-adherent cells expressing specific surface antigens and that are able to differentiate into osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondroblasts in vivo and in vitro.
source: Adipose-derived stromal cells (ASCs) are defined as plastic-adherent cells expressing specific surface antigens and that are able to differentiate into osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondroblasts in vivo and in vitro (Dominici et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The abundance of adipocyte progenitors/precursors that differentiate into adipocytes is an important determinant of SCAT expandability and functionality.
source: The abundance of adipocyte progenitors/precursors that differentiate into adipocytes is an important determinant of SCAT expandability and functionality.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about adipose tissue biology.

claim: Adipocyte-differentiated ASCs have a crucial role in lipid handling, adipose tissue expansion, and insulin sensitivity.
source: Adipocyte-differentiated ASCs have a crucial role in lipid handling, adipose tissue expansion, and insulin sensitivity (Palmer and Kirkland, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: With age, the frequency of ASCs decreases.
source: With age, the frequency of ASCs decreases (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A reduction in the ASCs proliferation rate might ultimately reflect cell senescence and might be involved in the onset of metabolic alterations (e.g. insulin resistance) observed during aging.
source: A reduction in the ASCs proliferation rate might ultimately reflect cell senescence and might be involved in the onset of metabolic alterations (e.g. insulin resistance) observed during aging.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the relationship between ASC proliferation, senescence, and metabolic alterations.

claim: The age-dependent senescence of ASCs has been linked to a decrease in mitochondrial activity and an increase in levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: The age-dependent senescence of ASCs has been linked to a decrease in mitochondrial activity and an increase in levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Choudhery et al., 2014; Maredziak et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some studies found that aging had a negative effect on adipocyte differentiation.
source: Indeed, some studies found that aging had a negative effect on adipocyte differentiation (Karagiannides et al., 2001; Murphy et al., 2002; Sepe et al., 2011; Caso et al., 2013; Beane et al., 2014), whereas others found that adipocyte differentiation increased with age (de Girolamo et al., 2009; Choudhery et al., 2014; Maredziak et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research showing conflicting results.

claim: Other studies found that adipocyte differentiation increased with age.
source: Indeed, some studies found that aging had a negative effect on adipocyte differentiation (Karagiannides et al., 2001; Murphy et al., 2002; Sepe et al., 2011; Caso et al., 2013; Beane et al., 2014), whereas others found that adipocyte differentiation increased with age (de Girolamo et al., 2009; Choudhery et al., 2014; Maredziak et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research showing conflicting results.

claim: Targeting senescent cells in adipose tissue will enhance adipogenesis and metabolic function in old age.
source: Lastly, it has been suggested that targeting senescent cells in adipose tissue will enhance adipogenesis and metabolic function in old age (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Different mechanisms were involved in physiological, in vivo, aging and in passage-related, in vitro, aging, resulting in different adipocyte dysfunction.
source: We show here that different mechanisms were involved in physiological, in vivo, aging and in passage-related, in vitro, aging, resulting in different adipocyte dysfunction.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings based on experimental data.

claim: At early passages, ASCs isolated from SCAT of aged donors displayed stress-induced senescence leading to early adipocyte mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cellular insulin resistance but preserved adipogenesis.
source: Thus, at early passages, ASCs isolated from SCAT of aged donors displayed stress-induced senescence leading to early adipocyte mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cellular insulin resistance but preserved adipogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: In vitro passage-induced aging in young-donor ASCs was responsible for the onset of senescence features in the absence of oxidative stress leading to a gradual decline in the proliferation and adipocyte differentiation capacity associated with enhanced insulin resistance.
source: Conversely, in vitro passage-induced (long-term in vitro culture) aging in young-donor ASCs was responsible for the onset of senescence features in the absence of oxidative stress leading to a gradual decline in the proliferation and adipocyte differentiation capacity associated with enhanced insulin resistance.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: All dysfunctions were more pronounced in aged-donors ASCs with increasing passage number.
source: Interestingly, we showed that all these dysfunctions were more pronounced in aged-donors ASCs with increasing passage number.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: Metformin is widely used to treat diabetes and also appears to modulate a number of aging-related disorders.
source: The biguanide drug metformin is widely used to treat diabetes and also appears to modulate a number of aging-related disorders (Barzilai et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Metformin exerts pleotropic effects and has a favorable influence on metabolic and cellular processes closely associated with the development of age-related conditions, such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and cellular senescence.
source: Metformin exerts pleotropic effects and has a favorable influence on metabolic and cellular processes closely associated with the development of age-related conditions, such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and cellular senescence.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about metformin's effects.

claim: Via the activation of AMPK, metformin exerted an antioxidant effect and improved mitochondria metabolism.
source: Our results show that, via the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), metformin exerted an antioxidant effect and improved mitochondria metabolism.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: Metformin alleviated the stress-induced cellular senescence of aged-donor ASCs and rescued adipocyte differentiation and function.
source: Therefore, metformin alleviated the stress-induced cellular senescence of aged-donor ASCs and rescued adipocyte differentiation and function, which might be involved in the drug's insulin-sensitizing effect in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: Metformin's effects might be involved in the drug's insulin-sensitizing effect in vivo.
source: Therefore, metformin alleviated the stress-induced cellular senescence of aged-donor ASCs and rescued adipocyte differentiation and function, which might be involved in the drug's insulin-sensitizing effect in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the clinical implications of the findings.

claim: The population doubling times (PDT) of young-donor ASCs at P7 and P11 were slightly longer than at P3.
source: The population doubling times (PDT) of young-donor ASCs at P7 and P11 were slightly longer than at P3 (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The mean percentage of senescent young-donor ASCs (i.e. those positive for senescence-associated (SA)-β-galactosidase) was increased at P7 and P11.
source: The mean percentage of senescent young-donor ASCs (i.e. those positive for senescence-associated (SA)-β-galactosidase) was increased at P7 and P11 (Figure 1C–D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The level of lysosome accumulation measured by Lysotracker fluorescence remained unchanged in young-donor ASCs across passages.
source: although the level of lysosome accumulation measured by Lysotracker fluorescence remained unchanged (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Young-donor ASCs expressed significantly greater levels of the cell cycle arrest proteins p16INK4 and p21WAF1 at P7 and P11 and of the senescence-associated protein prelamin A at P11 compared to P3.
source: Accordingly, young-donor ASCs expressed significantly greater levels of the cell cycle arrest proteins p16INK4 and p21WAF1 at P7 and P11 and of the senescence-associated protein prelamin A at P11 compared to P3 (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The level of ROS production in young-donor ASCs was the same regardless of the passages.
source: However, the level of ROS production was the same regardless of the passages (Figure 1H), indicating that oxidative stress was not enhanced in that setting.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Young-donor ASCs did not show any modification of mitochondrial mass over the passages.
source: Young-donor ASCs did not show any modification of mitochondrial mass over the passages (Figure 1I)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Young-donor ASCs presented a decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, mostly at P11 as compared to P3.
source: but presented a decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, mostly at P11 as compared to P3 (Figure 1J), in favor of late mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Long-term in vitro culture of young-donor ASCs induced the onset of senescence with mitochondrial dysfunction but without enhanced oxidative stress.
source: These data suggest that long-term in vitro culture of young-donor ASCs induced the onset of senescence with mitochondrial dysfunction but without enhanced oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: At P3, aged-donor and young-donor ASCs had similar proliferative abilities and thus a similar PDT.
source: At P3, aged-donor and young-donor ASCs had similar proliferative abilities and thus a similar PDT (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Aged-donor ASCs presented a mild senescent phenotype as compared to young-donor ASCs, characterized by a slight increase in senescent cell count, greater lysosome accumulation, and higher expression of p16INK4, p21WAF1, and prelamin A.
source: Aged-donor ASCs presented a mild senescent phenotype as compared to young-donor ASCs, characterized by a slight increase in senescent cell count, greater lysosome accumulation, and higher expression of p16INK4, p21WAF1, and prelamin A (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-G.

claim: The mild senescence in aged-donor ASCs at P3 was not associated with mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: This mild senescence was not associated with mitochondrial dysfunction (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I-J.

claim: A Seahorse experiment performed in young-donor and aged-donor ASCs at P3 did not reveal any difference in basal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and maximal respiration measured after the addition of FCCP.
source: In agreement, a Seahorse experiment performed in young-donor and aged-donor ASCs at P3 did not reveal any difference in basal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and maximal respiration measured after the addition of the uncoupling agent carbonyl cyanide 4-trifluoromethoxyphenylhydrazone (FCCP) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Unlike young-donor ASCs, aged-donor ASCs presented early oxidative stress.
source: It is noteworthy that, unlike young-donor ASCs, aged-donor ASCs presented early oxidative stress (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The PDT for aged-donor ASCs increased markedly from P5 to P11.
source: In contrast to young-donor ASCs, the PDT for aged-donor ASCs increased markedly from P5 to P11 (Figure 1A–B), indicating a steady increase in growth inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Cell viability did not change significantly over the culture period in aged-donor ASCs.
source: It is important to note that cell viability did not change significantly over the culture period (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown.

claim: Aged-donor ASCs presented a marked increase in SA-β-galactosidase activity, lysosome accumulation, p16INK4, p21WAF1, and prelamin A expression at P7 and P11.
source: Aged-donor ASCs also presented a marked increase in SA-β-galactosidase activity (Figure 1C–D), lysosome accumulation (Figure 1E), p16INK4, p21WAF1, and prelamin A expression (Figure 1F–G) at P7 and P11.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1C-G.

claim: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunctions were amplified over the passages in aged-donor ASCs.
source: Moreover, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunctions were amplified over the passages (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Only physiological aging led to senescence associated with oxidative stress.
source: Taken as a whole, these results show that only physiological aging led to senescence associated with oxidative stress and that during long-term in vitro culture, aged-donor ASCs expressed senescence earlier and more intensely than young-donor ASCs did.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: During long-term in vitro culture, aged-donor ASCs expressed senescence earlier and more intensely than young-donor ASCs did.
source: Taken as a whole, these results show that only physiological aging led to senescence associated with oxidative stress and that during long-term in vitro culture, aged-donor ASCs expressed senescence earlier and more intensely than young-donor ASCs did.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Increasing in vitro passage was associated with lower lipid accumulation in adipocytes differentiated from young-donor ASCs.
source: Increasing in vitro passage was associated with lower lipid accumulation in adipocytes differentiated from young-donor ASCs (Figure 3A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Lower lipid accumulation in adipocytes from young-donor ASCs occurred via a decreased expression of the pro-lipogenic and pro-adipogenic markers SREBP1c and PPARγ.
source: via a decreased expression of the pro-lipogenic and pro-adipogenic markers SREBP1c and PPARγ (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Adipocytes differentiated from young-donor ASCs presented a decrease in insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt at P7 and P11.
source: Adipocytes differentiated from young-donor ASCs also presented a decrease in insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt, a key enzyme involved in short-term metabolic responses to insulin, in favor of a cellular insulin resistance at P7 and P11 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: In vitro aging of young-donor ASCs, that resulted in ASC senescence, was not associated with early mitochondrial dysfunction in derived adipocytes (at P7).
source: Interestingly, in vitro aging of young-donor ASCs, that resulted in ASC senescence, was not associated with early mitochondrial dysfunction in derived adipocytes (at P7, Figure 3F and G), thus disentangling ASC senescence and adipocyte mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: At P3, adipocytes differentiated from young-donor or aged-donor ASCs had similar adipogenic capacities as shown by the similar triglyceride accumulation and pro-lipogenic and pro-adipogenic markers expression level.
source: Interestingly, at P3, adipocytes differentiated from young-donor or aged-donor ASCs had similar adipogenic capacities as shown by the similar triglyceride accumulation (Figure 3A–B) and pro-lipogenic and pro-adipogenic markers expression level (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Only adipocytes differentiated from aged-donor ASCs displayed enhanced oxidative stress.
source: By contrast, only adipocytes differentiated from aged-donor ASCs displayed enhanced oxidative stress (Figure 3E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Adipocytes differentiated from aged-donor ASCs displayed mitochondrial dysfunction characterized by increased mitochondrial mass and decreased membrane potential.
source: and mitochondrial dysfunction characterized by increased mitochondrial mass and decreased membrane potential (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The analysis of basal OCR in adipocytes differentiated from young-donor and aged-donor ASCs at P3 did not reveal any significant difference.
source: Moreover, the analysis of basal OCR, using Seahorse experiments, did not reveal any significant difference (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The adipocytes differentiated from aged-donors ASCs displayed a major decrease in their maximal respiratory capacity.
source: However, the adipocytes differentiated from aged-donors ASCs displayed a major decrease in their maximal respiratory capacity, as indicated by a significantly lower increase in OCR after the addition of the uncoupling agent FCCP (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Increased oxidative stress associated with mild senescence in aged-donor ASCs resulted in mitochondrial dysfunction in ASC-derived adipocytes.
source: Therefore, increased oxidative stress associated with mild senescence in aged-donor ASCs resulted in mitochondrial dysfunction in ASC-derived adipocytes, suggesting that adipocyte mitochondrial dysfunction could be linked to increased oxidative stress in ASCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Adipocyte mitochondrial dysfunction could be linked to increased oxidative stress in ASCs.
source: Therefore, increased oxidative stress associated with mild senescence in aged-donor ASCs resulted in mitochondrial dysfunction in ASC-derived adipocytes, suggesting that adipocyte mitochondrial dysfunction could be linked to increased oxidative stress in ASCs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Adipocytes differentiated from aged-donor ASCs presented decreased acute insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt indicating insulin resistance.
source: Adipocytes differentiated from aged-donor ASCs also presented decreased acute insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt indicating of insulin resistance.
evidence: This is based on experimental data measuring Akt phosphorylation.

claim: Throughout the passages, adipocytes differentiated from aged-donor ASCs presented altered adipogenic capacities, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction that were more pronounced as compared to adipocytes differentiated from young-donor ASCs.
source: Throughout the passages, adipocytes differentiated from aged-donor ASCs presented altered adipogenic capacities, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction that were more pronounced as compared to adipocytes differentiated from young-donor ASCs (Figure 3A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-G.

claim: Insulin resistance paralleled oxidative stress in adipocytes differentiated from aged-donor ASCs.
source: Insulin resistance paralleled oxidative stress (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: The senescence of ASCs, observed during the long-term in vitro culture, could be responsible for the altered adipogenic differentiation.
source: Altogether, these results support the hypothesis that the senescence of ASCs, observed during the long-term in vitro culture, could be responsible for the altered adipogenic differentiation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: The physiological aging that leads to oxidative stress in aged-donors ASCs at early passages would lead to enhanced metabolic alterations in adipocytes, but preserved adipocyte differentiation capacities.
source: By contrast, the physiological aging that leads to oxidative stress in aged-donors ASCs at early passages would lead to enhanced metabolic alterations in adipocytes, but preserved adipocyte differentiation capacities.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: A treatment for 30 days with lopinavir associated with a low dose of ritonavir (LPV/r) led to ASC senescence.
source: As shown in Figure 5, a treatment for 30 days with lopinavir associated with a low dose of ritonavir (LPV/r) led to ASC senescence (Figure 5A)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: LPV/r treatment led to marked oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunctions in ASCs.
source: but also to marked oxidative stress (Figure 5B) and mitochondrial dysfunctions (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Adipocytes derived from LPV/r-treated ASCs exhibited increased oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunctions together with altered adipogenesis.
source: Adipocytes derived from these LPV/r-treated ASCs exhibited increased oxidative stress (Figure 5E) and mitochondrial dysfunctions (Figure 5F–G) together with altered adipogenesis (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Induction of oxidative stress and senescence in young-donor ASCs results in severe adipose dysfunction in derived adipocytes.
source: This confirms that induction of oxidative stress and senescence in young-donor ASCs results in severe adipose dysfunction in derived adipocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the LPV/r treatment experiment.

claim: Darunavir associated with a low dose of ritonavir (DRV/r) did not increase senescence in ASCs but induced mild oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Interestingly, another PI with less adverse effects, darunavir associated with a low dose of ritonavir (DRV/r), did not increase senescence in ASCs but induced mild oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing DRV/r to LPV/r effects.

claim: Treatment of ASCs with DRV/r did not impede differentiation of derived adipocytes.
source: Accordingly, treatment of ASCs with DRV/r did not impede differentiation of derived adipocytes further indicating that mild oxidative stress in the absence of senescence in ASCs did not impair adipogenesis.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing preserved adipogenesis with DRV/r treatment.

claim: Mild oxidative stress in the absence of senescence in ASCs did not impair adipogenesis.
source: Accordingly, treatment of ASCs with DRV/r did not impede differentiation of derived adipocytes further indicating that mild oxidative stress in the absence of senescence in ASCs did not impair adipogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DRV/r treatment experiment.

claim: Metformin did not modify the PDT of young-donor ASCs.
source: As shown in Figure 6A–B, metformin did not modify the PDT of young-donor ASCs
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Metformin had no effect on the level of senescence or oxidative stress and a mild effect on mitochondrial dysfunction in young-donor ASCs.
source: and had no effect on the level of senescence or oxidative stress and a mild effect on mitochondrial dysfunction (Figure 6C–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-I.

claim: Metformin prevented the relative decrease in cell proliferation in aged-donor ASCs presenting stress-induced senescence.
source: Conversely, metformin prevented the above-mentioned relative decrease in cell proliferation in aged-donor ASCs presenting stress-induced senescence (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Metformin rescued the higher percentage of senescent cells, the greater lysosome accumulation, and the higher expression of cell cycle inhibitors p21WAF1 and p16INK4 in aged-donor ASCs at P11.
source: Accordingly, metformin rescued the higher percentage of senescent cells (Figure 6C–D), the greater lysosome accumulation (Figure 6E), and the higher expression of cell cycle inhibitors p21WAF1 and p16INK4 (Figure 6F) previously observed at P11.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: In aged-donor ASCs, metformin reversed the dysfunction associated with oxidative stress-induced senescence.
source: Taken as a whole, these data show that in aged-donor ASCs, metformin reversed the dysfunction associated with oxidative stress-induced senescence.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Metformin treatment reversed oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to the levels observed in young-donor ASCs.
source: Indeed, metformin treatment reversed oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to the levels observed in young-donor ASCs whereas it did not reverse senescence features in young-donor ASCs which do not display enhanced oxidative stress (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: Metformin did not reverse senescence features in young-donor ASCs which do not display enhanced oxidative stress.
source: Indeed, metformin treatment reversed oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to the levels observed in young-donor ASCs whereas it did not reverse senescence features in young-donor ASCs which do not display enhanced oxidative stress (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: Metformin was unable to rescue the altered adipogenesis observed in adipocytes derived from young-donor ASCs at P11.

claim: Metformin restored the adipogenic capacity of aged-donor ASCs at P11 to the level observed in young-donor ASCs.
source: Conversely, metformin restored the adipogenic capacity of aged-donor ASCs at P11 to the level observed in young-donor ASCs.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing improved adipogenesis with metformin treatment.

claim: Metformin treatment during the proliferation state increased lipid accumulation and increased C/EBPα, and SREBP1c expression in adipocytes from aged-donor ASCs.
source: Indeed, metformin treatment during the proliferation state increased lipid accumulation (Figure 7A–B) and increased C/EBPα, and SREBP1c expression (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Metformin pre-treatment lowered levels of oxidative stress in adipocytes-differentiated ASCs from aged donors.
source: Lastly, metformin pre-treatment lowered levels of oxidative stress (Figure 7G),
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Metformin pre-treatment led to a partial rescue of the insulin sensibility in adipocytes-differentiated ASCs from aged donors.
